title: From Chełmno to Auschwitz: the liquidation of Łódź’s ghetto
summary: The deportations and final liquidation explain the catastrophe that overtook the community and its surviving residents.

editorialContent:
## The ghetto’s changing population

For Łódź, liquidation was not a single moment in the summer of 1944. It was a sequence of deportations, pauses and renewed roundups that began in January 1942. The memorial book’s accounts connect that longer process to the fate of the [Łódź Ghetto](/communities/lodz/records/mention_64ff3d4392c1aaac689ee955), where residents were imprisoned and forced to work, and to a larger community whose population changed as Jews were brought in from other towns and regions.

Those arrivals mattered. The memorial book recalls Jews from [Pabianice](/communities/lodz/records/mention_5f115aab9927db3e659b878d), [Włocławek](/communities/lodz/records/mention_e83a3f4c8da842e9a04bf9d8), [Kalisz](/communities/lodz/records/mention_e70e915482e74a98ab4d2496), [Sieradz](/communities/lodz/records/mention_0b0ba3bfac23195ce3e4dea6), [Łask](/communities/lodz/records/mention_61271bde14547f0df5b31b28) and [Zduńska Wola](/communities/lodz/records/mention_2bbded12eb7ad02db0541e01), among others. It describes Jews from liquidated ghettos arriving in Łódź, and separately notes that some later arrivals were Polish Jews from nearby towns. The record does not give a complete list of people or dates for each arrival. Wider historical accounts establish the scale: in 1941–42, nearly 40,000 Jews were deported into the ghetto from German-occupied provincial towns and from Germany, Austria, Luxembourg, and the Czech lands. The crowded, already impoverished ghetto thus became a place of forced confinement for people displaced from many communities—not a refuge from Nazi persecution. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lodz?utm_source=openai))

## The first deportations to Chełmno

The memorial book dates the first transport from Łódź to [Chełmno (Kulmhof)](/communities/lodz/records/mention_5e2dbc350d3faa3562eae178) to January 16, 1942, departing from Radegast station. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum independently gives the same date for the start of deportations. Chełmno, about 70 kilometers from Łódź, was a killing center where German perpetrators murdered people using gas vans. In the memorial book’s account, children and thousands of others were deported and murdered there; it specifically recalls children as victims, not as an abstract category. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/1942-key-dates?utm_source=openai))

The January transports were followed by further deportations in 1942. The USHMM describes the September “Gehsperre” action, when German authorities targeted children, elderly people and the sick for deportation to Chełmno. These wider records help clarify what the memorial book’s references to children and other vulnerable people describe. The perpetrators were Nazi German authorities and police, not an impersonal fate: the memorial book names the [Nazi murderers](/communities/lodz/records/mention_fcbbe30f2798ed00d78dc055) as those responsible for deportations and killing. By autumn 1942, large-scale transports from Łódź stopped. The ghetto remained under brutal forced-labor conditions, but residents faced the continuing threat of starvation, disease and eventual deportation. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/give-me-your-children-voices-from-the-lodz-ghetto?utm_source=openai))

## Deportations resume, then the final evacuation

In June 1944, deportations resumed. The memorial book records the renewed transfers to Chełmno and then the movement of transports toward Auschwitz. The USHMM’s account specifies that more than 7,000 people were sent to Chełmno between June 23 and July 14, 1944, in ten transports; nearly all were murdered. The account also explains the deception used to secure compliance: people were told they would be sent for labor. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/chelmno?utm_source=openai))

Dates for the final phase vary across the records and sources. One supplied record dates the ghetto evacuation to August 8, while another describes the broader liquidation as occurring during the summer. The USHMM’s timeline places the final liquidation in August–September, and records the first transport’s arrival at Auschwitz on August 9. These accounts need not mean that everyone was deported on the same day: preparations, roundups and transports unfolded in stages. The memorial book remembers the [Gestapo](/communities/lodz/records/mention_47fba51d164a2145494cd208) and [Schupo](/communities/lodz/records/mention_c2b74a0d575ef8cefbf83b19) entering the ghetto as evacuation began. Their presence marks the coercive reality behind the official language of “evacuation.” ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1942-1945/liquidation-of-the-lodz-ghetto?utm_source=openai))

The memorial book’s testimony is direct and spare: transports arrived at [Birkenau](/communities/lodz/records/mention_695d588728b4b33bd4c96f4b), and Jews from Łódź were sent to [Auschwitz](/communities/lodz/records/mention_0b13dec1e28fc5b4544a392d). Wider records estimate that about 67,000 people were deported from Łódź to Auschwitz-Birkenau in August; the timeline notes that about two-thirds were murdered in the gas chambers on arrival. Figures differ across accounts, in part because they count different dates or groups: the final transports, the broader liquidation, or people moved elsewhere. The important distinction is clear: the Chełmno transports in June–July preceded the mass deportations to Auschwitz in August. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/timeline-event/holocaust/1942-1945/liquidation-of-the-lodz-ghetto?utm_source=openai))

## Those left behind—and what the records cannot restore

The deportations did not immediately empty the ghetto. A small group remained to sort possessions and clear the area. The USHMM estimates 1,000–1,500 people were left behind for this work; other accounts give different counts and describe people hiding or gathered in separate assembly camps. Soviet forces liberated the remaining prisoners in January 1945. The memorial book’s final image—hope turned into a march toward Auschwitz’s gas chambers—captures the destruction of communal life, but it cannot name everyone who was deported, killed, hidden or separated from family.

The ghetto’s changing population is part of this story, too. Those brought from nearby towns and from across Europe carried their own communal histories into Łódź; liquidation then scattered or destroyed those lives alongside the city’s Jewish community. The supplied memorial records name several places of origin but do not trace each arriving family through its fate. The ghetto registry, which recorded residents and sometimes deportation or death dates, also has a crucial gap: it did not record the fate of those deported in the final days. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/databases/Poland/LodzGhetto.html?utm_source=openai))

One question remains worth pursuing: whether the surviving records can identify more of the families transported from Włocławek, Pabianice and the other named towns—and distinguish those who arrived in Łódź from those who shared a surname but not a family connection. This is not a gap that the memorial book alone can close. Its testimony preserves what survivors remembered; independent archives and individual records may add names, but absence from one archive is not proof that a person or family was not there.
